Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the NovaVolt Automotive Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press * then 1 on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Lisa Patel, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Lisa Patel:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to NovaVolt Automotive's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Mike Harlan, CEO; Sarah Chen, CFO; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Mike Harlan.

Mike Harlan:
Thank you, Lisa, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 2024 was a pivotal quarter for NovaVolt Automotive. We made significant strides in key areas, including updates on our supply chain constraints and robust mitigation strategies, factory expansions paired with operational efficiency improvements, overall company performance highlights with record deliveries and profitability milestones, and gross margin expansion through scale and cost discipline. We are particularly excited about the upcoming launch of the NV-250 affordable crossover and its anticipated boost to our market share in the sub-$35,000 EV segment.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Chen to discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Sarah Chen:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning, everyone. I'm thrilled to walk you through what has been a transformative quarter for NovaVolt Automotive. Before diving deeper into the numbers, let me highlight our overall performance: we delivered record revenues, accelerated vehicle production, expanded our market leadership in premium and mass-market EVs, and made significant strides in battery technology and vertical integration. These achievements position NovaVolt not just as a player in the EV revolution, but as a leader driving sustainable mobility at scale.

Starting with the top line: Q3 revenue reached $2.82 billion, a robust 52% year-over-year increase and 18% quarter-over-quarter growth, smashing our guidance midpoint of $2.5 billion. This was propelled by 28,000 vehicle deliveries – up 67% YoY and exceeding our updated target of 27,000 units. Our core lineup, including the NV-Max sedan and the all-new NV-400 SUV, accounted for 72% of deliveries, with the NV-400 alone ramping to 12,300 units, capturing 15% North American market share in the electric SUV segment, ahead of competitors like Ford's Mustang Mach-E and Rivian's R1S.

Gross profit came in at $728 million, yielding a strong 22.5% automotive gross margin – a 420 basis point improvement YoY and well above our long-term target trajectory. Excluding regulatory credits, which totaled $156 million (up 30% YoY from IRA incentives and California ZEV mandates), our core margins expanded to 21.4%, driven by fixed-cost leverage from our Gigafactory Nevada ramp-up and a 15% reduction in battery cell costs through our in-house LFP-NMC hybrid cathode production. Vehicle average selling price held steady at $48,500, reflecting strong demand for our premium trims with standard 400-mile EPA range and Level 3 autonomy hardware.

On the bottom line, we posted GAAP net income of $312 million, or $1.24 adjusted EPS, versus a loss last year – our first profitable quarter on an adjusted basis since going public. Adjusted EBITDA soared to $456 million, with a 16.2% margin, underscoring our path to sustained free cash flow positivity, which we hit at $210 million this quarter. Cash and equivalents stand at $4.7 billion, bolstered by $750 million in fresh convertible notes at just 1.75% yield, reflecting investor confidence amid broader market volatility. Operating expenses were controlled at $450 million, balancing R&D investments with disciplined SG&A.

Key achievements this quarter merit special callout. First, production excellence: Our Gigafactory Nevada achieved 95% nameplate capacity utilization for 46-series cylindrical cells, producing 18 GWh – enough to power over 150,000 NovaVolt vehicles annually. This vertical integration cut our bill-of-materials by 22% YoY, insulating us from supply chain disruptions that plagued peers. We also broke ground on Gigafactory Texas Phase 2, targeting 100 GWh by 2026, with initial output focused on next-gen solid-state prototypes promising 600-mile range and 10-minute 80% charges.

Second, product innovation and launches: The NV-400 Launch Edition sold out its 5,000-unit allocation in under 48 hours, with real-world testing validating 520-mile highway range on our 800V architecture – outperforming Tesla's Model Y in WLTP cycles. We rolled out over-the-air (OTA) software update 2024.3.1 to 85% of our fleet, enabling unsupervised FSD Beta v12.2, which reduced disengagements by 40% per NHTSA metrics. In parallel, our NV-250 urban crossover hit 10,000 cumulative deliveries, dominating the sub-$50K segment with a 28 kWh LFP pack sourced from our partnership with CATL, achieving 5.2 miles/kWh efficiency.

Regionally, North America remains our fortress, contributing 68% of revenue with 19,400 deliveries – a 75% YoY surge fueled by $7,500 IRA point-of-sale rebates and our 22% market share in premium EVs above $80K MSRP in select trims. Europe accelerated to 22% of total deliveries (6,250 units), up 120% YoY, as we localized production at our Berlin plant to dodge EU tariffs on Chinese imports – now at 45% on BYD and SAIC vehicles. The NV-Max sedan's 320-mile range and CCS2 compatibility resonated in Germany and Norway, where EV penetration hit 28% of new sales. Challenges persist in China, where we delivered 2,800 units (10% of total) amid fierce pricing wars; however, our premium positioning yielded 35% higher ASPs than local rivals like NIO, and we're ramping local LFP production via our joint venture with Beijing Auto to target 20,000 units in FY25.

Strategically, we're doubling down on resilience and scalability. Our supplier diversification – now with 40% North American-sourced batteries versus 15% last year – mitigated cobalt price spikes (up 18% QoQ) and secured 1.2 million units of 2025 production. We announced a $1.2 billion framework with Panasonic for silicon-anode cells, aiming for 20% energy density gains by H2 2025. On the autonomy front, our Robotaxi pilot in Austin logged 250,000 autonomous miles with a 99.7% uptime, partnering with Waymo for HD mapping tech – a step toward our 2026 dedicated ride-hail fleet.

As we dive deeper into our Q3 results, I want to provide a comprehensive update on supply chain dynamics, which continue to be a critical factor in our operational performance here at NovaVolt Automotive. While the broader automotive sector grapples with persistent headwinds, we've made meaningful progress in derisking our supply chain, enabling us to deliver 28,000 vehicles in Q3—a 12% sequential increase despite industry-wide challenges. Let me break this down by key constraint areas, quantify the impacts, and outline our mitigation strategies, with a focus on both near-term execution and long-term resilience.

First, semiconductor availability. The chip shortage, exacerbated by lingering effects from the 2021-2022 crunch and ongoing geopolitical tensions around Taiwan, impacted our production by approximately 8% in Q3, down from 18% in Q2. This primarily affected our NV-400 SUV platform, where advanced SiC MOSFETs for our 800V architecture represent about 15% of our bill of materials value. ASPs for these chips remain elevated at around $4.50 per unit, 25% above pre-pandemic levels, contributing roughly 2 points to our COGS inflation. Regionally, we've seen variability: APAC-sourced chips from TSMC and Samsung improved 20% QoQ in lead times, now averaging 18 weeks versus 25 weeks in Q2, but European suppliers like Infineon continue to face allocation constraints tied to ID.4 and Audi e-tron ramp-ups.

Our mitigation here is multifaceted. We've diversified away from single-source dependency—NovaVolt now sources from five qualified SiC vendors, including emerging U.S. players like Wolfspeed, which supplied 15% of our Q3 needs under a multi-year offtake agreement. We're also accelerating our in-house ASIC development for power electronics, targeting a 30% reduction in external chip reliance by 2025 through custom designs optimized for our 400 kW peak powertrain. Inventory buffers stand at 14 weeks of supply, up from 10 weeks YoY, funded through our $2.5B revolving credit facility without straining liquidity—net debt to EBITDA remains at a healthy 1.8x.

Turning to battery materials and cells, this remains our most material exposure, accounting for 45% of our vehicle BOM. Lithium carbonate prices have stabilized at $45,000 per metric ton LCE equivalent, down 10% QoQ but still 150% above 2020 levels, driven by surging demand from Tesla's 4680 ramp and BYD's LFP dominance. Nickel sulfate spot prices hovered at $22,000/MT, pressuring NMC cathode costs. In Q3, raw material volatility shaved 1.2 points off our gross margins, with cell ASPs at $105/kWh for our 100 kWh packs—competitive with LG Energy Solution's prismatic cells but challenged by CATL's LFP pricing at $92/kWh.

Production-wise, battery constraints limited our output by 10% quarter-over-quarter, particularly for our high-nickel NV-500 sedan, where cobalt-free 811 cathodes faced delays from Indonesian smelter bottlenecks. Regionally, China-origin cells (60% of our mix) saw improved throughput post-COVID lockdowns, but U.S. IRA-compliant sourcing from our Nevada gigafactory joint venture with Panasonic only hit 70% capacity utilization due to graphite anode supply gaps from Synthetic Graphite suppliers.

Our strategies are yielding results. We've locked in 80% of 2024-2026 cell volumes through long-term contracts: 40% with LGES (U.S./Korea), 30% with CATL (China/Indonesia), and 20% domestic from Panasonic, qualifying for the full $7,500 IRA tax credit on 85% of our U.S. builds. Vertically, we're investing $1.2B in upstream integration—partnering with Piedmont Lithium for 50,000 MTPY spodumene from our Carolina project, securing 25% of our LCE needs at a blended $20,000/MT forward price. Technologically, we're shifting 30% of our lineup to LFP chemistries by Q4 2024, reducing nickel exposure by 40% and enabling cell-to-module architectures that cut pack costs 15%. Recycling initiatives with Redwood Materials are ramping, recovering 95% black mass purity from end-of-life packs, targeting 10 GWh recycled input by 2026 to offset virgin material costs by 8-10%.

On the logistics and rare earths front, Red Sea disruptions inflated ocean freight rates by 30% to $12,000 per FEU for APAC-to-U.S. routes, delaying 5% of our Q3 component arrivals. Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) for PM motors spiked to $85/kg amid Chinese export quotas, impacting our axial-flux motor suppliers.

Mitigations include air-freight bridging for high-value parts (e.g., 2,000 tons in Q3 at 3x cost but preserving 3,000 vehicle deliveries) and reshoring magnet production via a JV with MP Materials in Texas, derisking 50% of our NdPr needs. We're also piloting ferrite-assisted synchronous reluctance motors, reducing rare earth content by 70% without efficiency loss—prototypes tested at 98% peak efficiency.

Regionally, North America benefits from IRA incentives, with 75% localized content driving $450M in tax credits YTD. Europe faces headwinds from EU CBAM tariffs on Chinese batteries, prompting us to allocate 15% more capacity to our Berlin plant with Northvolt cells. APAC remains volatile but opportunistic, with our Shanghai SKD assembly capturing 20% China market share amid local protectionism.

Strategically, these challenges are accelerating our "Fortress North America" playbook: $4B capex through 2025 for U.S. cell gigafactories, supplier co-location parks in Georgia and Tennessee, and AI-driven supply chain visibility via SAP IBP and our proprietary digital twin platform, which improved forecast accuracy to 92% and reduced stockouts by 25%. We're on track for 120,000 units in FY24, with supply chain drag shrinking to under 5% by year-end.

In summary, while constraints persist, our proactive diversification, vertical integration, and tech innovations have insulated margins—Q3 gross margin hit 22.4%, up 180 bps QoQ—and positioned NovaVolt as a supply chain leader in EV.

This brings me to our factory expansions and operational efficiency improvements—two pillars that are driving our path to sustainable profitability and market leadership in the EV space. As you know, we've been aggressively scaling to meet surging global demand for our flagship models, the NV-400 compact SUV and the NV-Max long-range sedan, while navigating the choppy waters of supply chain volatility and geopolitical tensions. Let me break this down with the specifics.

First, on factory expansions. We're committing $4.2 billion in capex this fiscal year—up 28% from last year—to boost our global nameplate capacity by 65%, from 1.2 million units annually to nearly 2 million by Q4 2025. This isn't just about adding square footage; it's strategic vertical integration tailored to the EV megatrend.

Our crown jewel is the NovaGigafactory Nevada expansion, Phase II, which broke ground last quarter. This 2.5 million square foot addition will ramp to 150 GWh of LFP and NMC battery production by mid-2026, leveraging our proprietary 46-series cylindrical cells—think an evolution of Tesla's 4680 architecture but optimized for 20% higher energy density and 15% lower cobalt content. We're co-locating cell manufacturing with pack assembly to slash logistics costs by 12% per kWh, directly feeding our Reno vehicle plant. This positions us to capture IRA-compliant production credits, projecting $450 million in annual tax incentives once fully ramped—on par with what Rivian and Lucid are seeing from their Georgia and Arizona facilities.

Regionally, we're diversifying smartly. In Europe, our Magdeburg gigafactory—our first outside North America—is expanding by 40% to 100 GWh, with first packs rolling off the line next month. This is critical for EU Battery Passport compliance and localizing 80% of our supply chain amid the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). We're partnering with Northvolt on sodium-ion tech pilots here, targeting sub-$80/kWh costs to compete with BYD's Seagull in the sub-€25,000 segment. In Asia, we've greenlit a $1.1 billion joint venture in Thailand with local partner Bangchan, adding 500,000 units of CKD assembly for Southeast Asia and Australia. This hedges against U.S.-China tariffs, which spiked 25% on battery components last year, and taps into ASEAN's EV adoption boom—projected at 30% CAGR through 2030 per BloombergNEF.

We've also fast-tracked our Blue Ridge City campus in Tennessee, inspired by Ford's BlueOval model, integrating stamping, body-in-white, and final assembly under one roof. This 1.8 million sq ft mega-site will hit 400,000 units/year by 2026, creating 5,200 high-tech jobs and qualifying for $750 million in state incentives. Total expansion capex breaks down as: 55% batteries, 30% vehicle lines, 15% automation and testing. ROI modeling shows a 22% IRR over five years, with breakeven at 75% utilization—achievable given our order backlog of 320,000 units.

Now, shifting to operational efficiency improvements, where we're not just building bigger—we're building smarter. Our OEE—overall equipment effectiveness—has climbed from 82% to 91% YoY across our network, outpacing industry averages of 85% per the Automotive Industry Action Group benchmarks. This translates to a 17% reduction in cost of goods sold per vehicle, dropping from $28,500 to $23,600 on the NV-400 line.

Key initiatives include our "VoltFlow" digital twin platform, powered by Siemens Xcelerator and NVIDIA Omniverse. This AI-driven simulation has optimized weld cycle times by 22%, reducing NV-Max body-in-white defects from 1.2% to 0.4%—critical for our gigacastings, where we're adopting Giga Press tech akin to Tesla's, but with aluminum-steel hybrids for 15% weight savings. In painting and sealing, robotic vision systems from Cognex cut overspray waste by 18%, saving $12 million annually in materials.

On the battery front, we're implementing cell-to-pack (CTP) 3.0 architecture, eliminating 40% of module components versus traditional designs. This, combined with dry electrode coating pilots—licensed from 24M Technologies—has boosted throughput by 35% at our pilot line in Shanghai, targeting full rollout by Q2 2025. Energy efficiency is another win: LED lighting, heat pumps, and solar microgrids across sites have slashed Scope 1&2 emissions by 24% and utility costs by 16%, aligning with SBTi net-zero goals and unlocking EU ETS rebates.

Supply chain resilience is embedded here too. We've localized 65% of critical minerals sourcing—lithium from our Nevada brine JV, nickel from Indonesia via a Vale offtake—reducing lead times from 180 to 90 days. Just-in-time inventory via SAP IBP has freed up $280 million in working capital, with supplier scorecarding driving 11% average price concessions.

Strategically, these moves de-risk us against market headwinds. EV demand softened 8% in Europe Q3 due to subsidy phase-outs, but our efficiency gains let us hold ASPs steady at $48,200 while peers like VW cut ID.3 prices 12%. In the U.S., we're scaling ahead of the affordable EV wave—our upcoming NV-250 at $32k MSRP will leverage these efficiencies for 25% gross margins from Day 1. China remains hyper-competitive; BYD's 3 million unit run-rate pressures us, but our Thailand hub and LFP focus give us a 10% cost edge in exports.

Looking forward, Q4 guidance incorporates $1.2 billion in expansion-related ramp costs, but we expect 22% sequential production growth to 280,000 units, with EBITDA margins expanding 300bps to 14.5%. By 2026, these initiatives will deliver $2.8 billion in annual run-rate savings, funding R&D into solid-state cells and Level 4 autonomy.

Now, turning to our gross margin guidance and key assumptions, which remain a cornerstone of our path to sustained profitability in this dynamic EV landscape. As you know, gross margins in the automotive sector, particularly EVs, are heavily influenced by scale efficiencies, raw material pricing volatility—especially battery metals like lithium carbonate, nickel sulfate, and cathode precursors—supply chain localization, and product mix shifts toward higher-margin platforms.

For the third quarter, we delivered a non-GAAP gross margin of 22.5%, up 420 basis points year-over-year and 250 basis points sequentially. This outperformance was driven by several factors: first, our Shanghai Gigafactory hitting 85% utilization on the NV-Max platform, which shaved $1,200 per unit off COGS through optimized gigacasting and structural battery packs; second, a favorable mix with 35% of deliveries being our premium NV-400 Long Range variant, boasting a 28% segment margin versus 18% for base models; and third, battery cell costs declining 18% YoY to $85 per kWh, thanks to our vertical integration with our Nevada cell gigafactory ramping to 20 GWh annualized output using prismatic LFP/NCM hybrid chemistry.

Looking ahead, we're tightening our full-year 2024 non-GAAP gross margin guidance to 24% to 25%, from our prior 23% to 26% range. This reflects stronger-than-expected Q4 volumes of 120,000 units—up 45% YoY—partially offset by seasonal FX headwinds in Europe and one-time warranty provisions related to our early NV-400 truck fleet. Key assumptions here include:

Average Selling Price (ASP): Holding at $48,500 globally, supported by disciplined pricing in the U.S. where federal IRA incentives add $7,500 per vehicle on average for our North American content exceeding 60%. We're lapping softer pricing from last year amid intensifying competition from Tesla's refreshed Model Y and BYD's Seagull exports.

COGS per unit: $37,200, down 12% YoY, anchored by 46-series cylindrical cell adoption reducing pack costs to $90/kWh at scale. We've locked in multi-year offtakes for lithium hydroxide at $12,000/tonne, 30% below spot, via partnerships with Albemarle and Ganfeng.

Factory utilization and fixed cost leverage: Blended 82% across our U.S., China, and Germany plants, with Shanghai at 92% driving the lion's share of margin expansion.

Product mix: 40% premium trims (NV-400 LR/AWD and NV-Max) by year-end, up from 28% today, as we phase out entry-level RWD sedans in favor of our next-gen ME3 skateboard platform.

For fiscal 2025, we're guiding to non-GAAP gross margins of 27% to 29%, implying 300-350 basis points of expansion. This is predicated on delivering 450,000 to 500,000 vehicles—a 55% CAGR from 2022—fueled by NV-400 volume ramp in the U.S. and Europe, plus initial NV-250 deliveries exceeding 50,000 units.

Key 2025 assumptions and drivers:

Cost-down initiatives: Targeting $32,000 COGS per unit by H2'25 through 25% battery cost reduction to $65-70/kWh via dry electrode coating (similar to Tesla's Berlin progress) and silicon anode integration in 20% of packs; Giga-press adoption across 70% of body-in-white, cutting stampings by 40% and material waste by 15%; Supplier localization: 75% North American content for U.S. plants to maximize IRA credits up to $7,500 LEAP + $3,750 battery components.

Regional commentary: U.S. (55% of volumes): Margins at 30%+, bolstered by IRA tailwinds and tariff protections (100% on Chinese LSVs). We're gaining share in the $50k+ SUV segment against Rivian R1S and Ford F-150 Lightning, with Q4'24 promotions fully absorbed. Europe (25%): 22-24% margins amid EU tariffs (up to 45% provisional on BYD/Chinese OEMs) but pressured by weak demand and VAT rebates phasing out. Our Berlin plant's unibody aluminum architecture keeps us competitive versus VW ID.4. China/APAC (20%): 25% margins as cost leader, leveraging Shanghai's efficiencies against CATL-supplied rivals like NIO ET5. Export headwinds to ASEAN offset by domestic fleet deals.

Risks and offsets: Upside from regulatory credits ($500M expected) and FSD-like autonomy hardware attach rates hitting 25%. Downside risks include lithium spot prices rebounding above $15k/tonne (our hedge covers 60% exposure) and UAW labor inflation adding $400/unit in the U.S. We're mitigating via automation capex of $1.2B, targeting 95% robot density.

Strategically, this guidance underscores our "Scale or Fail" mantra—echoing Tesla's playbook but with diversified regional footprints to de-risk China dependency. By Q4'25, we expect automotive gross margins approaching legacy OEM levels (GM/Ford at 12-15%) while preserving EV premiums through software margins (target 60% on autonomy subscriptions) and energy storage cross-sell.

We're confident in execution, with line-rate tests on ME3 platform completing next month. Our guidance for next quarter is Q4 revenue of $3.1-3.4 billion, full-year deliveries of 115,000-120,000 units representing 60% YoY growth, and 2025 capex of $2.8 billion focused on expansions and autonomy compute. Now, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press * then 1.

Analyst 1:
Hi, team, great quarter. Can you provide more color on the NV-250 launch timeline and how it factors into your affordable EV strategy amid softening demand?

Mike Harlan:
Thanks for the question. The NV-250 is on track for U.S. production start in Q2 2025, with initial deliveries by summer. It's built on our ME3 platform for $32k MSRP, leveraging LFP packs and gigacasting for Day 1 25% margins. This positions us to capture the mass-market wave as IRA rebates make it effectively sub-$25k for many buyers, targeting 100,000 units in year one without cannibalizing our premium lineup.

Analyst 2:
Sarah, on Europe—how are you navigating subsidy phase-outs and CBAM tariffs? Any adjustments to Berlin capacity allocation?

Sarah Chen:
Solid question. Europe's subsidy cuts did soften Q3 demand by 8%, but our Berlin expansion to 100 GWh with Northvolt sodium-ion pilots keeps us agile. We've shifted 15% more capacity there for CBAM compliance, hitting 80% localization. Margins hold at 22-24% via unibody efficiencies, and we're gaining versus VW ID.4. No major reallocations needed; Thailand JV hedges APAC exports.

Analyst 3:
Mike, with $4.2B capex this year, what's the updated 2025 capex outlook and ROI thresholds for new sites like Tennessee?

Mike Harlan:
Capex peaks at $4.2B in 2024 but moderates to $2.8B in 2025, with 55% on batteries. Tennessee's Blue Ridge City targets 22% IRR at 75% utilization, backed by 320k backlog and $750M incentives. We're prioritizing high-ROI vertical integration, like Nevada Phase II, to support 450k-500k deliveries without liquidity strain—cash at $4.7B gives us ample flexibility.

Lisa Patel:
Thank you for your questions. We have time for one more.

Analyst 4:
Sarah, on gross margins—what's the biggest risk to your 27-29% 2025 guide, and how hedged are you on lithium/nickel?

Sarah Chen:
Margins are resilient, but lithium rebound above $15k/tonne is a key watch item—we've hedged 60% via fixed offtakes at $12k/tonne with Albemarle. Nickel via Vale. Upside from $500M credits and 25% autonomy attach. Automation counters UAW costs. We're on track for 300bps expansion through scale and 25% cell cost cuts to $65/kWh.

Operator:
Thank you. I would now like to turn the call back to Mike Harlan for closing remarks.

Mike Harlan:
Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us today. We are confident that NovaVolt Automotive is well-positioned for continued success in the rapidly evolving automotive landscape. We look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter.

Lisa Patel:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes the NovaVolt Automotive Q3 2024 earnings call. You may now disconnect.
